utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May it please Mr. President, Your Honours. I, along with Mr. Daryl Mundis and Ms. Ruth Karper, appear on behalf of the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stamp. And appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, Stefane Bourgon, co-counsel, and Mirna Milanovic, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Mr. Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone in the courtroom, the representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence, the accused, and everyone else in the courtroom, in particular, the Registrar, who disappeared for a few days and is now back. We have a number of witnesses who will be heard today. Before we start examining the witnesses, the Trial Chamber would like to remind both parties that when a decision is rendered, it is necessary to listen to the decision so that the interpretation is followed by the parties. Because if we comment on a decision after a decision has been rendered, this could give rise to confusion. As far as the Judges are concerned, Article -- Rule 86 of the Rules of Procedure must be respected -- Rule 46. Rule 46, not 86. As well as the code of practice for the lawyers, which governs the rules to be followed when exercising one's profession. In the future, when an oral decision is rendered, it should be listened to and it shouldn't be commented on while the decision is being rendered. I'll now turn to Mr. Mundis. There are two witnesses on the schedule for today. Could we call the first witness into the courtroom. But Mr. Mundis or Mr. Stamp, who is the first witness you are going to call?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Mr. President, for whom an application we would want to make in private session will have to be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Registrar. We will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness ZJ, early in the morning on the 8th of June, 1993, was there an attack upon the area that you were deployed in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who attacked, and from where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The BH army, from the direction of the Bosniak villages, Mehurici, Suhi Dol. In fact, from Zenica, they went to Brajkovici from Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you when the attack started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Bukovica, Velika Bukovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this attack, I take it it was against the HVO units in your area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My colleague has just asked an extremely leading question. He told him that this attack was directed at HVO units in his area. The attack could have been conducted in a number of areas. And the Prosecution should have at least allowed the witness to answer this question himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stamp, you have taken note of the comment, according to which the question was leading, and the witness could only have provided one answer to the question. But you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was really trying to be as economical as I could on time, which is almost precious as it here [sic]. I did not know that that issue was in -- was contested at all. That is why I thought it was a permissible leading question. But I'll be more careful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your units, that's the HVO, did the lines hold or did they have to retreat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I knew, the resistance was very slight. The resistance against BH attack, BH army attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did your lines hold firm, or were you forced to retreat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as each village fell, or as the soldiers withdrew, that is what happened in each village. In fact, they didn't resist. There was some sporadic shooting, as far as I could notice. That's what the defence consisted of.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to speak more loudly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that Mr. ZJ. Could you speak a little more loudly, and if you can, directly into the microphone. Did you and your company retreat to any town in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We withdrew to the territory of Nova Bila, that is to say, we later established a line in the place called Cifluk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About when did you establish the line at Cifluk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was in the afternoon. In fact, the consolidation lasted for a few days. On the same day, on the 8th of June, is when I think we established these new lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Incidentally, just for the record, Cifluk is C with a hat diacritic, I-F-U-K [sic]?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where is Cifluk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Cifluk is about two and a half kilometres, as the crow flies, from Guca Gora, about two and a half kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you established your line at Cifluk, about what time of the afternoon was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's difficult to say. It was difficult to realise that in all the confusion, because there were civilians who were carrying on, going on to Busovaca, Novi Travnik, and Vitez. So it's difficult to determine what the exact time was, but it was about 5.00, 6.00, or 7.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you personally went there to the lines at Cifluk, was it dark out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not completely. But as I said, there was a lot of confusion at the line itself, because the conflict was ongoing. So one didn't have much time to think about what wasn't very important at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Cifluk, could you see into Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you in a position to say what is the condition of the houses in Guca Gora at the time when Guca Gora was captured by the attackers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We looked through binoculars. On the following day, we observed more frequently, because on the day, there was still fighting. I know that all the houses had been burnt down, apart from one or two, perhaps; the houses were intact [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there's an important mistranslation. The witness -- he's listening to what I'm saying - said that apart from two or three houses which had been set on fire, all the other houses were intact on the following day. According to the translation, the witness said the reverse. He said, according to the translation, that all the houses had been set on fire on the following day. So the translation is quite the reverse of what the witness stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stamp, could you clarify this matter. Ask the witness who observed Guca Gora through the binoculars from a distance of two and a half kilometres. Can you ask him what he saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you heard what counsel said. I saw you nodding. Is it correct that you said that apart from two or three houses that had been set on fire, the other houses were intact after Guca Gora had been captured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The other houses were intact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was up until the next day, the day after, the 9th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that day, the 9th of June, did you observe anything happening to those houses from your lines at Cifluk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the first day, I noticed -- in fact, it was on the 9th. I noticed that Jozo Tavic's house was on fire. And on the following days, I think there were about 10 or 20 houses. Maybe during the first 15 or 20 days, that's when they set fire to the greatest number of houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how about the contents of these houses? Do you know anything about them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did the contents of the houses remain in the houses or were they taken away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My house is below the monastery, and naturally, when I observed through the binoculars, I looked at the central part. We saw a number of lorries there. They were covered, and looting was probably what was happening. And during the following ten days, the lorries drove around. There was a lot of traffic in Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to ask you just for a little precision, just to help me with precision. You're saying that these things you saw during the following ten days, the ten days following which date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the 8th of June, that is to say, when the BH army took Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you saw lorries which were covered. Did you notice any markings on any of these lorries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They were civilian lorries. At the time, I don't remember there being any military markings on lorries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said looting was probably happening. That is a translation I have. Could you tell us exactly what you saw in relation to looting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, we saw those two lorries. A lot of people were moving around. There were a lot of large and small lorries driving around. That's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see these people doing anything or transporting anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's difficult to say. It's difficult to say with certainty what the people were doing, but what would unknown people be doing in Guca Gora? What would they be doing setting fire to houses and probably taking things that were of use? This is what one could assume.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said many of the houses were set on fire. What became -- what happened to your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My house was also set on fire. My house and everything in the surroundings. It was almost impossible to see that houses had been there, at least the first time that we returned to that location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see who it was who set the houses on fire? And I'm not asking you if you saw individuals that you could identify, but are you able to tell the Court if these individuals belonged to any particular organisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the BH army. Because after the BH army attack, after the place had been taken, naturally, no other units could have appeared, for example, units from Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is a Franciscan monastery in Guca Gora; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know if, after the attack, any civilians, any Croat civilians, were taken there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found out about that on the 9th of June, when members of the international forces brought in civilians from the monastery who had remained in part of Guca Gora, which was by the Bosniak village of Krpeljici. They remained there. There was a lot of confusion then and panic. And later they placed them in the monastery. Naturally, when members of the international forces evacuated them on the following day, they evacuated them to Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what international force that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: SFOR, UNPROFOR. I don't know. I don't really remember. In various periods of time, the names were different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That's the examination-in-chief, may it please you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stamp. I just have one matter I would like to clarify, Witness. You said you were two and a half kilometres away, and apparently, you followed what was happening over a number of days. The people who were present, were they aware of the fact that there were people observing them at a distance of two and a half kilometres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know. One could assume so, because we were familiar with this territory, and it was very easy to assess the situation. We had a line of sight. Both parties had a line of sight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So those who were there were aware of the fact that you were not very far away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume so, because throughout the entire war, we were attacked. They knew where our lines were very well. So I don't doubt that they were aware of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll now turn to the Defence for their cross-examination. I would like to point out that we are in open session, so you should ask to go into private session when you think it is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay, Mr. President. I would now like us to go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, around March 1992, is it true that the Serbs occupied Mount Vlasic and that the local population started to panic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct also, Witness, that following the establishment of the front line by Serb forces, members of the protection force for the village of Guca Gora were assigned there in turn to spend shifts of one to two days there, to take turns? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At first, only members of the company from Guca Gora. Afterwards, people came from Nova Bila and other locations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was only later, in the spring of 1992, that the Guca Gora company was formed through the regrouping of the protection force in your area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like us to go back into private session just for one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We're going into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was in this period of time, Witness, that the Travnik brigade was formed --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. Let me repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness ZJ, it was during this period that the Travnik Brigade was formed and the Guca Gora company started reporting to the commander of the battalion in Dolac, more specifically, to the commander, Ivo Bajo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Witness, in this period, relations between the Croat and Muslim communities were good in Guca Gora; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness ZJ, during the second part of 1992, and the beginning of 1993, in the territory of Travnik and in the area of Guca Gora, there were a large number of refugees that started arriving; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These refugees were coming from Jajce, as well as from other villages. From the west and north-west of Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these refugees, Witness, were coming because they had been expelled and they arrived without any possessions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume so. I'm not an expert to tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it true to say that with the fall of the town of Jajce, when Serb forces took up positions defended by the HVO and the BH army, the inhabitants of Jajce, as well as those who were defending that town, also arrived in the area of Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also true, Witness, that among those refugees, there were individuals and groups who had arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it also true, Witness, that some of those persons joined the BH army during 1993 and slowly started to organise themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, they all joined the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you agree that they organised themselves little by little in the course of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't follow at all, nor did we have any contact with them, because they were mostly in Bosniak villages, and I do assume that they did organise themselves, that is, that they joined the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. During this period, would you agree with me in saying that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the process of formation, as well as the HVO, didn't really have the kind of uniforms that one would expect of a regular army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also true to say, Witness, that in fact people were wearing what they had, that is, some of them had complete camouflage uniforms, whereas others only had parts of camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, Witness, that during this period, there were individuals who were neither members of the HVO nor members of the BH army, but were still wearing parts of camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but they were in the minority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Do you agree with me that about March 1993, relations between the Muslim and Croat communities were tense, to such a point that you started digging trenches around the villages of Guca Gora and try and establishing positions there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And among those trenches, Witness, you dug trenches towards the villages of Krpeljici and Han Bila; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Trenches were being dug towards the villages from which there were minor conflicts, because of those trenches, because trenches were being dug on both sides, and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Is it true that the Frankopan Brigade, which replaced the Travnik Brigade, was created on the 1st of April and was under the command of Ilija Nakic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also true, Witness, that this brigade consisted of units which were deployed, among others, in Guca Gora, Brajkovici, Nova Bila, and Puticevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also true, Witness, that the headquarters of the brigade for the period between April and May 1993 was situated in the Guca Gora monastery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the monastery. Yes, within the compound of the monastery, but in an old auxiliary building within that compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this building was attached to the main monastery, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also true, Witness, that at the end of May 1993, commander Nakic decided to relocate the headquarters of the brigade to Nova Bila, leaving behind him in this building attached to the monastery a communications and an operations centre? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I didn't really pay much attention, but some kind of communications centre was left behind, but just of a formal nature. As I was saying, nothing was left of the brigade except for a signalsman, who didn't really have any importance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Is it also correct to say that you established checkpoints on the roads leading to the village of Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Everything was under a blockade. The Bosniaks and the Croats couldn't establish contact for these reasons, perhaps from the last days in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, I don't know whether you received the interpretation of the last sentence. That is why I was waiting. I will continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. As you said, at that time, things were under a blockade and the BH army had to use that road to go from Travnik to Zenica and from Zenica to Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, were you aware of the fact that at the time the other road that could be used to go to Zenica was the one that went via Vitez and Busovaca, through the Lasva Valley, and at the time it couldn't be used by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume that's the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know that one of the checkpoints established by the HVO was in the centre of the village of Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It wasn't in the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the checkpoint wasn't in the centre of the village, could you tell us where exactly the checkpoint was located, the checkpoint through which one could gain access to the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as in all the other villages, at the entrance and exit of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, are you aware that on the 2nd of June, 1993, at the checkpoint through which one could gain access to Guca Gora, the commander of the Bosanska Krajina operations group, Mehmed Alagic, was arrested, disarmed, and only following the personal intervention of Colonel Blaskic and of the international forces was it possible for him to be released?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know that during the same period, at the same checkpoint, through which one could gain access to Guca Gora, four buses, transporting BH army members who were going to positions at the front lines facing the Serbs in Turbe, they were arrested at this checkpoint, these members of the military arrested them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know where the checkpoint was, where Mehmed Alagic was arrested. That surprises me. But as for those members, we were afraid. We stopped them because we didn't want them to deploy their forces in the village. I know that 20 men stopped them there. At that time, I think either in Vitez or Travnik, there was shooting. So naturally, there was fear of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness ZJ. In response to my last question, you mentioned that the arrest of Mehmed Alagic surprised you. Is it my question that surprised you or is it the fact that Mehmed Alagic was arrested in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It's the arrest of Mehmed Alagic that surprised me, because I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness ZJ. Before we go on to the events that took place in June, there are certain things that I would like to check with you. They concern geographical matters in Guca Gora. You said a minute ago that the distance between Cifluk and Guca Gora was two and a half kilometres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, about two and a half kilometres. This is a rough estimate. It could be three kilometres. As I said, about two and a half kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness ZJ. And the distance between Nova Bila and Guca Gora, would you agree with me that it's a little over seven kilometres as the crow flies, naturally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, but I could assume so, because Cifluk is between Guca Gora and Nova Bila. And in territorial terms, it used to belong to the Guca Gora municipality, or parish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness ZJ, if I show you a map, would that help you to confirm the distance was seven kilometres between Nova Bila and Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to go into private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go into private session, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Given the time, it's necessary to have our break now. It's 10 to 4.00. We'll have our usual 25-minute break and we'll resume at 4.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have about ten more questions for the witness after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, you have the floor again for the remaining ten questions that you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness ZJ, when you left for Guca Gora in the morning, you met some civilians, as well as soldiers, on the road, which were going for Bukovica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The soldiers and civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat what he said, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you say anything else in addition to: "Yes, soldiers and civilians"? Did you say anything else that the interpreter didn't understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the village of Radonjici, both civilians and soldiers. Yes, from the village of Radonjici. INTERPRETER: That's what he said

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And you tried, in view of the strategic importance of Radonjici, to convince the soldiers to defend the village, but you didn't succeed, and you all left for Nova Bila; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because at first I didn't have proper insight into the situation. But when I saw that houses were already burning in the village of Radonjici, and I saw large numbers of members of the BH army who were numerically stronger than we were, so I realised there was no chance for defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And once you arrived at the headquarters of the brigade in Nova Bila, that you were able to receive information regarding the situation in Guca Gora; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not quite, because I was following what was going on over the radio. The batteries were dying. I couldn't use it, but I could receive information on it. And I knew that the village of Maljine had also fallen to the BH army. So I heard that there was panic in Guca Gora, and that was a logical reaction to what was happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was then that you left with a group of soldiers from your unit towards Cifluk; and from there, you were able to see that the village of Guca Gora had been taken without any damages?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't know if that's a question or if he's repeating the evidence. That is not the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it was a question. I'm asking the witness whether it is true that, from the headquarters of the brigade in Nova Bila, he left again with members of his unit towards Cifluk, from where he was able to observe that the village of Guca Gora had been taken, without any damage being done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that right, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't go to the headquarters, and no members of my unit were with me. I was alone. And en route to Sarici, going towards Guca Gora, I was joined by two or three boys, or soldiers, who I didn't really know and who went with me to Guca Gora. And we met the civilians and some soldiers near the village of Radonjici. And another group of soldiers and civilians stayed behind in a part of Guca Gora, in an area called Rajici towards Krpeljici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you confirm, Witness, that when you were able to observe the village of Guca Gora, which had been taken, the village had been taken without any damage being done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Nothing was burning. It was quiet. There was silence. All efforts were focussed on the transportation of civilians, because when I arrived, they were in a clearing which was exposed to the fire from the BH army. And on the side were trenches of the BH army members from the village of Radonjici. So that I did my best to have the people cover this section of the road unharmed, as far as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Did you have anything to add to your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see the word Radonjici, but not Radonjici. The village is Radojcici. These are two different localities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Thank you for this clarification. My question is the following: You know that the next day, international forces, UNPROFOR, undertook the evacuation of a large number of civilians who took refuge in the monastery of Guca Gora? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Witness, that among the people who were killed during the attack on Guca Gora, on the basis of the rumours that you heard, you said that there were two who were not members of your unit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement, you mentioned that the fact that the name of a person may be on a list of people receiving financial aid does not necessarily mean that that person was a soldier at the time of the facts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are also aware, Witness, that this was a normal practice during the conflict, that is, to place names of killed people on lists of soldiers so that the families could receive financial aid; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether that was the practice, but I do know that I did so myself, for purely social benefit reasons. As for how other people acted, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Following the evacuation by international forces of the people in Guca Gora, it was only the next day, that is, the 10th or 11th of June, that you saw houses on fire in Guca Gora; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also true that the distance between you and those houses at that point in time was about three kilometres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I was saying, about two and a half to three kilometres, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Even with your binoculars, you were not able to see whether the people who you could see in Guca Gora were civilians or military people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also true that you couldn't tell the difference between an older or a younger person, a man or a woman, and that you were not able to identify any military insignia on the people that you could see in Guca Gora? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness ZJ, when you answered questions from my learned friend, you gave two answers. First you said unknown people were in Guca Gora, and a second time you said that they were members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is it true, Witness, that the only reason why you said that, according to you, they were the BH army was a conclusion on your part and not something that you yourself saw with your own eyes? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. Are you talking about the period following the attack on Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Witness. The period following the attack. The days that followed after the evacuation by international forces. You said a moment ago that they were unknown people who were looting, and then later on, you specified that they were members of the army. I submit to you that when you said that they were members of the army was simply a deduction on your part and not something that you yourself saw. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the two months that followed the attacks and the conflicts in Guca Gora, you were able to see several houses that were set on fire; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Witness. During the two months that followed the events in Guca Gora, you were able to see from a distance several houses that were set on fire; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. For the first 15 days or so, several houses were burning, and afterwards, sporadically, maybe one would be set on fire, and then nothing for several months. But the main burning of houses occurred in the first 15 days following the attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness ZJ, in your statement, you mentioned that up to 1995 even, houses continued to be set on fire in Guca Gora; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that one was set on fire, I think, in 1995. I only heard about that. On the BH army days. And the house was owned by Tomo Vujanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement, you also said that between June 1993 and autumn 1997, the date when Croats could again feel safe in Guca Gora, more than 70 per cent of the villages had been destroyed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, would you agree with me in saying that it is not possible to say exactly when those houses were burnt, how they were set on fire, and who set them on fire? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you. It is common knowledge that the BH army had control of the area, captured the area, and they were responsible for the burning and everything else. If they couldn't prevent it, if they didn't do the actual burning, then they could have prevented it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. But you personally did not see members of the army setting fire to houses in Guca Gora; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness ZJ, I don't know whether you were able to receive any funds to reconstruct your own house, but on behalf of the Defence, I hope you will, most sincerely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. No question on your part? I turn to Mr. Stamp once again. Is there any re-examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There is, Mr. President, just one or two matters of clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session. We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that, Mr. President. I keep forgetting where exactly we are. I'd respectfully ask that that part be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, let us redact this and go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That you said within the compound of the monastery, the headquarters of the Frankopan Brigade, in April and May of 1993, was in an old auxiliary building within the compound, and you later on said that it was attached to the monastery. What do you mean by that, that it was attached to the monastery? Was it or was it not attached to the monastery building? Or was it a detached auxiliary building within the compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe the term was not quite accurate. It was a separate building, and it was not attached to the monastery building. It was a detached building.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Another matter for clarification. You said that from your observations -- or may I just start again with that question. You said in respect to my friend for the Defence, that from your observations, Guca Gora had been taken without any damage being done. And I believe you said, when I was asking you questions, that you observed two to three houses damaged when it was captured, at the time when it was captured. Can you explain that to us, if there's a conflict or if not? Could you just explain exactly what you mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said at the beginning that two or three houses were damaged, and there was smoke coming from them. I said that at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Mr. President, that the whole answer was not translated, because he said that two or three houses were damaged and that he could see smoke coming from them, but he added: "I don't know whether it was from a shell or from ..." And then he didn't finish his sentence. And this part of his answer was not translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Stamp, perhaps you should ask him the question again for the answer to be complete, because the Defence tells us that the English translation did not include a part of his answer, that is, what was the generator of the damage. So it would be best for you to put the question to the witness again and for the witness to answer your question with precision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You heard the exchanges now, Witness. Can you say how the two to three houses were damaged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is hard to tell. I couldn't establish that from Bukovica, or anywhere else, when we were going towards Radonjici, there is a better view. There were shells falling. One could hear the shelling. So I think in the area of Rajici there were two or three flames. Now, whether they were caused by a shell or by incendiary bullets, because these were also used widely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. And you said the main bulk of houses were destroyed in the first 15 days after the attack. Can you estimate about how many houses form that main bulk of the houses that were destroyed within 15 days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that about 200 buildings in all, in Guca Gora itself. There may be more, because there were stables, auxiliary buildings burning. But in Guca Gora, I would say there were, in all, about 300 housing buildings, so about 200 to 250 were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And just to be clear. The focus of my question is also in respect of the time these buildings were destroyed. Does your answer relate to the first 15 days after the attack of 8 of June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I'm saying in all, for the whole period. I don't have the exact figures, how many houses, how many other buildings, but that would roughly be the total number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Now, are you able to help us? If you can, that would be very good. If you can't, just say so. About how many houses - and you may approximate - but about how many houses were destroyed in the first 15 days after the attack? You did tell us that the bulk of the houses were destroyed in that period. Can you estimate about how many houses were destroyed in that 15-day period after the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the figure would be around 200 buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And just for clarification: Would those -- would all of those 200 be houses, or do you include other structures within the term "buildings"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm talking about dwellings, houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is it, Mr. President, may it please you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, we are now in open session. I would like to thank you for having answered the questions put to you by the Prosecution and by the Defence. We wish you a good trip home. I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom, but we will first lower the blinds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said that these were curtains and there are blinds behind you which are going to be raised, because there is a gallery. The public gallery is behind you. Could you stand up, please, and tell me your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Ivica Kegelj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 15th of September, 1957.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The village of Dusina, in Zenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Can you now tell me what your current profession is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a safety inspector in the Stevens Transport Company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In 1993, ten years ago, what was your profession at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd finished the secondary metallurgy school in Zenica in 1976, and from 1976 I worked in the Zenica ironworks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Have you already testified before the Tribunal or is this the first time you have come to testify before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As this is the first time, you have to make a solemn declaration. This is what one has to do when testifying. I would like to ask you to read the text in your own language, the text that is before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down. I'll provide you with some information about the proceedings, about the testimony you will be giving. The Prosecution, to your right, will put a series of questions to you in a minute. You will answer their questions. When they have concluded their examination-in-chief, Defence for the accused, who are to your left, will also ask you a series of questions. They will conduct what we call their cross-examination. The three Judges sitting before you might also ask you some questions in order to clarify certain issues. As you have made the solemn declaration and sworn to tell the truth, you should not lie, because if you do lie, that constitutes false testimony. And if you give false testimony, penalties could be imposed on you. You could either be fined or sentenced up to seven years in prison. In addition, as the proceedings conducted here are particular, if, when a question is put to you, you provide information that might be used against you, you may in such a case refuse to answer. Or if the Trial Chamber forces you to answer the question, in such a case, the information you provide can't be used against you. It's a little complicated, but I had to explain this. If you don't feel well, tell us, and we will adjourn immediately. Is everything fine? Have a little water. Can we continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kegelj. Can you please tell -- can you please tell the Trial Chamber what town or village you were living at -- living in in late 1992/early 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: I was living since my birth in the village of Dusina. From my birth up until 1993, throughout that period, that is where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, were you employed in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: No. Until 1993, I was registered in the company, but for a year prior to that, I was laid off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In January 1993, what were you doing? How were you keeping yourself occupied?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: I was in the HVO. I think I started in 1992. I was in the HVO army. We kept guard duty in the village and we received salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Witness, what -- did you have a rank in January 1993 as a soldier in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any rank. I was just a foot-soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us that you kept guard duty in the village. What village are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: At first, we kept guard duty together with the BH army. For a couple of months. And then, due to certain differences, we split. So we kept guard of our neighbourhood and the BH army kept guard duty in their area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Witness, when you make reference to "our neighbourhood," what neighbourhood are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: The village itself is divided. On the right side was a neighbourhood consisting of six Croatian households and two Serb households; and to the left side was a Muslim village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes. My question might not be clear, Witness, but what village are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Oh, I see. The village of Dusina. In the village of Dusina itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than performing guard duty in Dusina, what were your responsibilities in the HVO, if any?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: No. I didn't have any. We just kept guard duty and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In January 1993, as a soldier in the HVO, were you assigned to a particular unit? And if so, what was the name or number of that unit?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: The HVO. It was just the HVO. I don't know whether there was any number of a unit. It was the area of Lasva, Visnjica, and Dusina. And this is the unit that we belonged to as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall the name of your commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Zvonko Rajic. He was in charge of the area of Lasva, Visnjica, and Dusina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How many HVO soldiers were there in Dusina in January 1993 on a more or less permanent basis?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but I think seven or eight, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where did these seven or eight HVO soldiers that were guarding Dusina live? Where did they live?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: They all lived in houses in Dusina, in their own neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were the seven or eight HVO soldiers in Dusina in January 1993 organised into any type of shifts or otherwise structured?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: We had shifts. We would be on duty for 24 hours, two of us. And then later, we would go in fours. And before the 26th of January, the entire neighbourhood, all the HVO soldiers were on duty non-stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of clothing did you wear when you were on duty as an HVO soldier in Dusina in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: I had a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of weapons did the HVO soldiers in Dusina have in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: We had automatic rifles, Kalashnikovs, and we had a couple of semi-automatic rifles, and one M-48 rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned before the 26th of January the entire neighbourhood, all the HVO soldiers, were on duty non-stop. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened on the 26th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Two or three days prior to that, we noticed large groups of BH army troops concentrating in the villages, and then our commander, our leader, reported to the commander, Zvonko Rajic. However, Zvonko said that we shouldn't worry, that he had made an agreement with the BH army, that there would be no problems, and that, therefore, we shouldn't try anything, that we should just keep quiet and that nothing would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there, Witness. You told the Trial Chamber about large groups of BH army troops concentrating in the villages. What villages were you referring to when you said that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: I was referring to the area of Brdo, the lower part of Dusina, and the eastern or left side of Dusina, the Muslim part of the village, and also on the north, large numbers of soldiers were noticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what happened on the 26th of January, 1993 in Dusina.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: On the 25th of January, in the evening, we were on duty until midnight. After midnight, some soldiers went home to sleep. I stayed on in the house in which we were on duty. It was a Serb house which was more or less in the centre of the Croatian part of the village. And after midnight, we all fell asleep. There was no one on duty. In the morning, around 5.00 or 6.00 a.m., I was awakened by the shooting, as were the other soldiers. We all jumped up and we ran outside. I fled to the basement of that house. Others fled to the garage. There was a garage right next to the house. And I saw, coming from the north side, strong BH army forces, and just then I could see them chasing civilians out of their houses and shepherding them to Stipe's house. When we ran out, an HVO soldier from the village of Brdo, and who was with us that night, he was wounded. He was lying on the snow. He cried out that -- saying that there was a sniper shooting from the Muslim part of the village. We helped this Blasko, who was a -- Blasko Bosnjak. We carried him to the garage. We carried a blanket from the house and wrapped him in it. The sniper had hit him in the leg. In the meantime, soldiers were coming from the north side, who were in a column, approaching us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, let me interrupt you for just a moment. You mentioned civilians being shepherded to Stipe's house. Who is Stipe?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Stipo is my uncle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What is his surname or family name?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Stipo Kegelj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How many -- at the time the shooting started at 5.00 or 6.00 in the morning, how many HVO soldiers were in the Serb house?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: There were six or seven of us, so that two or three -- I don't know exactly where they went. I think they went to help the civilians, but I don't know. When we were surrounded, there were only four of us there. And Blasko, who was wounded, which makes it five in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us that you carried Blasko in a blanket back into the house. After you returned to the house, how long did you and the other HVO soldiers remain in that house?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: No. I just went into the house to get the blanket. Then I came out. We wrapped Blasko in the blanket and we carried him to the garage. We stayed in the garage. I didn't go back into the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the garage with the other HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Maybe some 15 minutes or so. In the meantime, these forces were approaching from the north, and we were forced to surrender. We didn't open fire. We didn't do anything. Augustin Rados, an HVO soldier, went out and said: We're surrendering. Don't shoot any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately what time on 26 January 1993 you surrendered in the village of Dusina?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Well, about 6.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How many HVO soldiers surrendered on that morning in Dusina?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: All of us surrendered. I know that there were the four of us who surrendered. As for the civilians and the other HVO soldiers, I didn't see them. They were over there, probably near Stipe Kegelj's house. I couldn't see them, and I don't know when they surrendered over there. There were quite a number of civilians in my own house as well. But I don't know that. I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what happened to you and the other HVO soldiers after you surrendered.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: When Augustin Rados said that we were surrendering, someone from the BH army said that we should come out one by one with our hands up, and that is what we did. We came out one by one. And they ordered us to come closer, so we did come up to them with our hands up. We came right up to them. We were ordered, all four of us, to lie down on the snow on our stomachs. And then they searched us to see whether we had any weapons or something like that. Then we got up. Once we got up, someone said that we had a wounded man in the garage. And then all four of us went up to the garage. One of the soldiers brought a stretcher. So we put Blasko Bosnjak, who was wounded, on the stretcher. Now, I don't know who it was who ordered that two men should carry Blasko, in the direction of their village, that is, the Muslim part of the village. And I was the first, and Mladen Kegelj. I picked up the stretcher. I was the one carrying -- no. Mladen Kegelj was in front. I'm sorry. He carried the stretcher in front, and I at the back. The soldiers around us were hitting us and pushing us around, so that I received many blows in the back and my legs. I don't know what they hit me with. And they ordered us to run as quickly as we could, run, run, as fast as we could, up to the centre of the Muslim part of the village, and the distance was about seven to eight hundred metres, and that is what we had to do, to run and carry the stretcher. When we reached this part of the village, I saw Esad Barucija's house, where the headquarters was, and there were some doctors or assistants - I don't know - from some sort of medical corps in that house. So we put the stretcher down 20 or 30 metres away from the house. Somebody took it over and carried him away. Then the four of us were there, and two others who came behind us. And we stood there for maybe some 10 minutes or so. Then one of the soldiers ordered us to take off our shoes. And then we stood there barefoot on the snow for 10 or 15 minutes. Then someone again gave us orders to put on our shoes. They cursed us, saying all kinds of things. We had HVO markings on our clothing, and the soldiers tore them off. I know that somebody pulled me by the ear, saying that he would cut off my nose. And things like that. Then someone again gave us orders to put on our boots again, and then there were other orders telling us to go back. And then they took us back from the Muslim part of the village to the crossroads itself between the Croatian and Muslim parts of the village. And at the very crossroads, I saw all the civilians who had been captured that morning. They were from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kegelj, let me interrupt you and ask a few questions in terms of clarification. You've mentioned the names of Augustin Rados and Mladen Kegelj as being among the HVO soldiers who surrendered. Do you remember - in addition to yourself, of course - do you remember the names of the other HVO soldiers who surrendered in Dusina on the morning of 26 January 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: When I surrendered, there was myself, Milenko Rajic, Augustin Rados, Blasko Bosnjak, and Mladen Kegelj, the five of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You also mentioned, later, two others joined you. Do you remember -- you said two others who came behind us. Do you remember who the other two individuals were?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand the question. Out of the HVO soldiers, there were five of us at that point. Later on, all the other soldiers who were captured in another village, or rather, in the same village but in another house, or next to another house. Later on, all the troops and all the civilians, all were captured and all were brought to this crossroads between the two neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you: You've told us about being ordered to take off your boots and then being ordered to put your boots back on. Do you know who it was who gave these orders?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: No, I don't know. One of the soldiers of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I have no idea who it was. I just know that someone ordered us to take off our boots, and after some time, it could have been one of the commanders who ordered us to put them back on. But just then, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Kegelj, what unit or units the soldiers to whom you surrendered were a part of?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: I don't know. On that day, I saw many different types of soldiers, and I didn't know them. I knew of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As for the rest, I did not know or recognise the other types of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Kegelj, I believe when I interrupted you, you were telling us about being brought to the crossroads between the two neighbourhoods. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what happened after you were taken to that crossroads.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Yes. At that crossroads, the entire Croatian population that had been captured that morning was there. They were all there in one spot. This was a crossroads between the Croatian part of Dusina and the Muslim part of Dusina. There was shooting around us. Soldiers were opening bursts of fire. And just then, someone said: My uncle -- told my uncle's wife that her son had been killed. Then she fainted, and the soldiers again were opening fire around us, telling us to keep quiet, not to shout or we would all get killed. Later on, five or ten minutes later, we were ordered to head towards our village. As we were going there, I saw a neighbour of mine, Hakanovic -- Edin Hakanovic. He was there, and he said: I have joined the BH army to assist and to be in charge of this operation, and I guarantee that no harm will come to you. I know that that is what he said. And then he said: We are going up to Brdo, because the village of -- in the village of Brdo there are some more HVO soldiers who haven't surrendered. And he said that the captured soldiers who can walk should go there, whereas the women and children and the elderly should go to Stipo Kegelj's house. And that is how we got to the crossroads leading to Brdo. That is where we separated. I was designated to be part of the human shield going to the village of Brdo, which is about seven to eight hundred metres away. And we walked, escorted by BH army soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kegelj, approximately how many BH soldiers escorted you and the surrendered HVOs as you proceeded towards the village of Brdo?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: I don't remember the number of soldiers there were. There may have been seven or eight of us, or six. And then about 20 or 25 civilians. So there were roughly 30 of us in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us a few moments ago that Edin Hakanovic said the women and children and elderly should go to Stipo Kegelj's house. Did they in fact go there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They went there, because we separated there. My wife and children went in that direction, in fact, and I went towards Brdo, to serve as a human shield, as I was ordered to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How many civilians went with you towards Brdo?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: I think 20 to 25. I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. I'm about to go into an area that I think might take us past the next scheduled recess. I might suggest this might be a nice time to take the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have the break and we will resume the hearing at 10 past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you may now continue with your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kegelj, right before we took the recess, you were telling us about being ordered, with the other HVO soldiers, to march or walk up towards Brdo. Did you in fact go to Brdo on the 26th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Yes. As I had been ordered, and I was escorted by BH army troops. I don't remember how many of them there were. Perhaps 20 of them. They escorted us to the Brdo village so that other inhabitants in the village of Brdo could surrender. When we got to the Brdo village, we were stopped by a house, the first house at the entrance of the village to Brdo, and we saw HVO soldiers on the hill that was opposite us. And then a woman called Zdravka Rados said: I'll now call my husband, who's on the other side of Brdo. He's in the HVO. She called out to Dragan Rados and the other soldiers and said that we had all been arrested and that we had to go in their direction and to serve as a human shield. And she said that they should surrender. They had to surrender too. So she called out. She called Dragan, her husband, for about five minutes. And from the opposite hill, I could see that the HVO soldiers - there were six, seven, or eight of them. I don't know how many. Six, I think - I saw them coming down the hill one by one, and they also surrendered. They descended into the valley. They surrendered, but I didn't see what happened to them after that. After they had all surrendered, we were returned. We were ordered to go back towards Stipe Kegelj's house, which is where we had come from. We were all returned to Stipe Kegelj's house, all of us who had served as a human shield, returned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kegelj, let me just stop you before you continue, to clarify something. The six HVO soldiers that you saw on the other side of the hill, you told us they descended into the valley and that you didn't see what happened after that. Did those six soldiers go with your group back to Stipe Kegelj's house?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: No. I only saw them come down from the hill, and they probably surrendered. I know that they surrendered. But I didn't subsequently see the direction they were taken away in. I know nothing about this. But the people who had served as a human shield were all sent back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, with respect to the six HVO soldiers on the other side of the hill, you said that they surrendered. Do you know to whom they surrendered?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: I don't know exactly who they surrendered to or how they surrendered. I don't make any distinctions. I know the BH army, but I'm not familiar with other units. All I know is that they surrendered. I'm only familiar with the BH army insignia, but I hadn't seen any other insignia at the time. So I really don't know which units participated in this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber, if you remember, the approximate time that you arrived back at Stipe Kegelj's house with that group, after having gone up to Brdo.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Well, I think it was about 10.00 or half past 10.00. About 10.00 in the morning, or perhaps it was half past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please --

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Perhaps it was half past 10.00.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what happened once you arrived back at Stipe Kegelj's house sometime between 10.00 or 10.30 in the morning on the 26th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: We were all returned to the house. All the civilians and soldiers had been placed in two rooms. They were overcrowded. I saw two to three soldiers in the house who guarded us. They were members of the BH army. They guarded us. And around the house, on several occasions, some soldiers opened fire. They made threats. They used bursts of fire and broke windows. They said all sorts of things. They then entered the house, opened bursts of fire, directed at the ceiling. They made threats, said all sorts of things, and so on, and then they went out again. And I know that about every hour, the soldiers who were with us inside would rotate. They would be replaced by other soldiers. They -- some of them were courteous. Others spoke in a different manner, they behaved differently. Some of them entered the house. They searched for weapons. They asked us to hand over weapons. And perhaps we spent about -- perhaps we remained in the house until the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kegelj, let me stop you there again to clarify something that you've said. You told us that all the civilians and soldiers had been placed in two rooms. My question is: Were the civilians and the soldiers mixed together in these two rooms, or were the civilians in one room and the soldiers in a different room?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: We were all mixed up. The civilians and soldiers were together. You could go from one room to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many civilians were in Stipe Kegelj's house in total between the two rooms?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Well, I think there were between 40 and 45 of them, if you take the soldiers and civilians together. That's how many of them there were in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of the other HVO soldiers who were in Stipe Kegelj's house on the 26th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: I was there, Milenko Rajic, Augustin Rados, Mladen Kegelj, Stipo Kegelj, Vinko Kegelj, Niko Kegelj. There was someone called Vojislav Stanisic, a civilian; another civilian whose name was Franjo Kristo. And the other people were women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you told us a few moments ago that you remained in the house until the afternoon. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what happened on the afternoon of 26 January 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: The guards rotated all the time, and during that period of time, I and some other soldiers - I can't remember who - on one occasion I was taken outside, in front of the house, placed by the wall. They asked me to tell them where our weapons were, where our PAMs and PATs were. And after I had been interrogated, I was returned. On a second occasion I was taken out again, maybe for about half an hour, and the questions they put to me were similar. And then opposite Stipe Kegelj's house, I saw Vinko Kegelj's house. I saw some soldiers who had let the livestock out, and I saw five or six soldiers who opened bursts of fire directed at the pigs. And then someone from that group of soldiers ran up to us. He put a rifle to my head. He wanted to fire, but he didn't. We were then returned, sent back into the house. And after that, I stayed in the house for perhaps another half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kegelj, let me again stop you. How many times were you taken out of the house and interrogated on that afternoon, in total?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Twice in total. The third time was when they took all the men out of the house. There were eight of us. The soldier Milenko Rajic wasn't taken out on that occasion. And eight of us were taken out of the house on the third occasion. We were then ordered to go in the direction of my house, which is about four or five hundred metres from Stipo Kegelj's house. We were escorted by a group of eight to ten men. Our hands were raised. We had our hands behind our heads, like this. We were then taken to my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kegelj, let me just again briefly ask you to clarify something for us. I want to return to the two occasions when you were taken out and interrogated. Who interrogated you, if you know, on either of those occasions?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: No, I don't remember who interrogated me. One of the soldiers, perhaps one of the BH army officers. I can't remember. I can't remember whether he had a rank. I can't remember which unit he belonged to. I can't remember this exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us that you were taken to your house. Do you recall approximately what time on the 26th of January, 1993 you arrived at your house with the other HVOs and the ABiH escorts?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: It was about 4.00 in the afternoon, between 4.00 and half past 4.00. All the men were then taken outside in front of the house. We were lined up there. Our hands were raised. And there were soldiers who were present. There were probably eight to ten of them from the BH army. They were our escort and they were taken to my house, which is four or five hundred metres away. The column was then stopped in the road in front of my house. That road leads from Dusina towards the village of Merdani. We were stopped in the road, and then one of the soldiers said that he was the commander of that unit. He said that his nickname was Geler, or "shrapnel." And he pointed to a glass eye that he had. He had lost an eye in Croatia a year or two ago, a year or two earlier. He issued orders himself. He asked us to hand over our weapons. He asked us where our PAMs and PATs were. He wanted information from us. We told him that all the weapons that we had had had been handed over. We told him that we didn't have anything else. And he immediately ordered one of his soldiers, and he singled out Augustin Rados, who was standing next to me. The others were behind me. He told him to leave the column, to step out of the column. And a soldier of his shot Augustin Rados at a distance of two -- from a distance of two or three metres. He opened a burst of fire from an automatic rifle. He fell down next to me. He was dying.
