He was making some sort of grimaces. And then I noticed that Geler ordered another burst of fire to be opened to kill him so that he'd stop grimacing. He then ordered the body to be removed from there immediately Two soldiers - I don't remember this exactly, but I think I was ordered and another person was ordered to move him. And then Geler behaved as if nothing had happened. He said: If you don't admit where your weapons are kept, this is what's going to happen to you. Then it was probably my turn, because I was the second person in the line. He also asked me about weapons, and I said that we didn't have Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. anything, apart from the rifles that we had handed over. I told him that we didn't have anything else. He then punched me in the head, in the stomach, in the legs. I fell down to the ground. There were some bricks behind me. I fell down on them. I got up. I didn't resist. I was covered in blood. There was blood covering my face. I got up. I was in a state of shock. I was afraid. I couldn't think straight. I realised what was going to happen to us. I realised why we had been taken there. And then Geler skipped me. I remember Stipo Kegelj was next to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kegelj, let me again interrupt. I apologise for that, but I have a couple of questions. First of all, at the time he was shot, do you know approximately how old Augustin Rados was?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Augustin Rados was born in 1964. I'm certain. He was about 28 or 29 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And at the time, was he a civilian or a soldier?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Yes, he was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you were ordered to move his body. Do you remember where you were told to place that body?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: As the body was on one side of the road, we were told to move it to the other side of the road, since there was a bank there, and we were told to move the body there so that it didn't obstruct the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you told us that after you moved the body, you were then beaten. Can you tell the Trial Chamber where you and the other surrendered HVO soldiers were after this beating?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: On one side of the road, where Augustin Rados had been killed, since when we had moved the body to the other side of the road, as the garage was on the other side of the road, Geler then ordered us to go to the other side of the road so that we couldn't see Augustin Rados's body. We were moved to the side where the bank was, but the garage prevented us from seeing this. I was at the edge, so I was able to see the body. I was closest to the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber where the surrendered HVOs were standing in relation to the garage?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: The back was facing the garage and my house, because my house was behind the garage. The backs were turned to the garage, the HVO soldiers' backs were turned to the garage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And were you part of this group of the HVO soldiers with your back to your garage?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Yes. I was there. But I was the first one in line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Just so that we're clear, Mr. Kegelj: When you say the first one in line," if you were facing the line, would you be on the left or on the right of the line? Someone facing, that is, looking at the line of the HVO soldiers, would you be on the right-hand side or on the left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: I was the first on the left-hand side. I was the first person, and to the right of me, all the other soldiers were to the right of me, and the civilian or the two civilians who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber, if you remember, the names of the other persons who were in that line with you on the afternoon of 26 January 1993. And, if you remember, the order that they were standing next to you, to your right.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: I was the first in line. Stipo Kegelj was next to me. And I can't exactly remember the order. I know that -- I think Niko Kegelj was there, Vinko Kegelj, Vojislav Stanisic, Pero Ljubicic, and I'm certain that the last person in line was Franjo Kristo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kegelj, do you know the approximate age of Niko Kegelj on that day?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: I think Niko Kegelj was 52 or 53 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And was he a soldier or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: He was a soldier. But in the village we had soldiers who were on standby. They were elderly people. Whereas the active-duty soldiers were younger. The elderly people were on standby. The only difference was that we would go on guard duty, but the older people didn't. They just had weapons that they kept in their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And was Niko Kegelj one of the standby soldiers or was he one of what you've called the active-duty soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Niko did not keep guard duty. He was on standby. He wasn't active.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kegelj, do you know the approximate age of Stipo Kegelj on the 26th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Stipo Kegelj was born in 1930, so he was 63 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At that time, was Stipo Kegelj a soldier or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: He was a soldier, but a standby soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kegelj, do you know approximately how old Vinko Kegelj was on the 26th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: I think he was 50, maybe 48. I think he was born in 1948.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was Vinko Kegelj a soldier or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: He was a soldier, but also on standby.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, on the 26th of January, 1993, the approximate age of Vojislav Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: I think he was about 70 years old, maybe even 71.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time, was Vojislav Stanisic a soldier or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: He was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate age of Pero Ljubicic on the 26th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Pero Ljubicic, I think, was about 65 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was he a soldier or a civilian at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: He was a soldier, but also on standby.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Kegelj: Do you recall the approximate age of Franjo Kristo on the 26th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: He was also over 60, maybe 61 or 62.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And was Franjo Kristo a soldier or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: He was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Kegelj, can you please describe, to the best of your recollection, what happened to the group of HVO soldiers, including yourself, that were lined up with your back to your garage on the afternoon of the 26th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: As Augustin Rados was killed, and when Geler himself beat me, some five or ten minutes after that, I was -- I almost fainted. I was semiconscious. Then he left me alone and passed on to Stipo Kegelj. He interrogated him too, and Stipo said that we had no weapons, like the rest of us. Then he ordered him to go along a path towards my house, below the garage. He ordered him to take this path, and Augustin Rados's body was on that path. I could see that. The man went unwillingly, slowly. And I just saw a burst of fire hitting him in the back. So he fell down the slope, and after that I didn't see him again. Then I think there was Niko Kegelj who was next, and the same happened to him. He was also killed with a burst of fire in the back. I know that Geler's soldiers were joking and vying for the opportunity. And when Geler ordered someone to go along that path, they kept saying: I'll fix this one," or "I'll fix that one." And then after Stipe, I think it was -- to the best of my recollection, it was Niko Kegelj's turn, after him came Vinko Kegelj, who was also questioned about weapons. And I remember well that when he asked Vinko Kegelj where the weapons were, Vinko told him: If I had -- we had weapons, and if I knew that they were dug 50 metres deep into the ground, I would tell you. I wouldn't give you my life. And then Vinko was killed in the same way, in the back, like the others, with a burst of fire from an automatic rifle. Then it went on like that. I think it was Vojislav Stanisic. And I think Pero Ljubicic was the last one. When Franjo Kristo's turn came, Franjo Kristo said: I am a civilian. I don't belong to the HVO. I'm a civilian and I come from another village. Then Geler said: That's enough. We won't continue. And he ordered me and Franjo Kristo, who were left, he ordered us to go back, under escort, to the house again. Once we returned to the house, Geler took out some sort of a diary, a notebook, and he wanted to interview me, if you could call it that. I don't remember what he asked me and what I answered. Geler was absolutely cold-blooded, as if nothing had happened. I gave him a statement, and then maybe half an hour after that statement, someone walked into the house, someone entered and called Geler to come outside, or to the corridor in the house. He told him something, and then Geler said: You two come out again. Franjo and myself went out, and then he told two soldiers: Go with them to remove the dead, the bodies of the dead. I know that two men escorted us, and a neighbour from the village, a young guy of 16 or 17. He too had a rifle. I don't remember his name, but he was referred to as Pide. He volunteered. He asked Geler: Can I go with them as well? And Geler said: Okay. Go along. That he should be the third to escort us. When --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kegelj, let me just stop you for one moment. On the 26th of January, 1993, when you saw him, do you recall what Geler was wearing?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: He wore a camouflage uniform. I didn't notice anything else in particular, any insignia of rank. I don't even remember whether he had a patch. Because I was out of my mind. I don't remember anything in particular. I just remember that he had a glass eye, and he explained this to us. Nothing else in particular. He was rather short, shorter than me, maybe 1 metre, 65 in height. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you remember anything Geler said to you after you returned to Stipo Kegelj's house?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Yes. He said to me, to me and Franjo: If we were to say anything to the civilians or anyone else, that he would have special treatment for us, that he would kill us, but in the worst possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kegelj, you mentioned the 16 or 17-year-old neighbour from your village, referred to as Pide. Do you know what ethnicity Pide was?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Well, he was a Muslim. However, four or five years prior to that, his mother remarried someone from that village. So he came from another village, and his mother remarried someone in the village. I think it was Elvid Mehmed, known as Omer. So his mother had married this man three or four years prior to this. So I only know this young man's nickname, which was Pide. I don't know his first or last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what happened when you and Franjo Kristo and Pide were taken out of Stipo Kegelj's house, where you went and what you did.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: I and Franjo Kristo went out, and then Geler said that two of his soldiers should escort us and this Pide. So there were three soldiers escorting the two of us. And he ordered us to collect the corpses and put them away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kegelj, when you say "the corpses," what corpses are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: The bodies of the six men who had been killed, executed, half an hour or an hour previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You also said that you were ordered to put the corpses away. Where were you told to put the corpses?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: When we got there, we were ordered to put all those bodies into my garage. Actually, the garage was on one floor, and then there was a kind of basement of that garage. There was a narrow area inside, so that the two of us put or threw those six bodies into the garage, one on top of the other. And that morning, there were two HVO soldiers in front of my house who were killed early in the morning, so there were six dead bodies plus the other two who had been killed and who were lying in front of my entrance all day. So there was a total of, all together, eight bodies in my basement. Franjo and I threw eight bodies into that basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What did you do after putting the bodies in the basement?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: I remember that I asked neighbour Pide, while we were doing this, I said: What is happening? What is going on? He didn't give me an answer. And then, as I had a lot of blood on my boots from the bodies, on my boots and my trousers, then one of the soldiers ordered me to clean it well. All I could do was to use the snow to clean the blood. And then we were turned back to Stipe Kegelj's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kegelj, approximately what time did you return to Stipe Kegelj's house after moving those corpses?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: I think that it was already dark by then. Around 6.00, 5.30 to 6.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: After you returned to Stipe Kegelj's house about 5.30 or 6.00 in the evening on the 26th of January, 1993, how long did you remain in the house?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Together with the civilians, Franjo and I stayed in the house until I think around 9.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where did you go when you left Stipe Kegelj's house that evening?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Around 9.00 in the evening, we were ordered that they had to transfer us to the elementary school, or rather, we were ordered to come out and, escorted by their soldiers, we didn't know where we were going. We were just ordered to come out of the house and to take the route towards the Muslim area. So we crossed the centre and reached halfway into the Muslim part of the village, escorted by their soldiers. Then I saw strong forces, I don't know how many, but a lot of soldiers. It was already night-time, and they were coming back from the village of Dusina. They were in the Muslim part of the village and along the whole road, units were lined up, moving towards Lasva. I don't remember how many there were. I know that there were three of us then, me, Franjo Kristo, and Milenko Rajic. Milenko Rajic, throughout that period, was in the house with the civilians. So the three of us were handed over to a unit - I don't remember which - to escort us or to take us with them in the direction of Lasva. They tied us up then with our hands behind our backs, with some sort of rope, and, escorted by this unit, I know that Milenko Rajic was up front; behind him, a BH army soldier; then me; then behind me, another soldier; then Franjo Kristo and another soldier. And we formed such a line and we went in that line to Lasva, which is about three kilometres away along that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When the three of you, that is, Franjo Kristo, Milenko Rajic, and yourself - left Stipo Kegelj's house, where were the civilians?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: I don't know anything about the civilians. When we left, they stayed behind in the house, so I don't know anything. I saw those civilians again. Actually, we were taken up to the school. We were untied in front of the school. We entered the school. In one classroom, I saw HVO soldiers from Visnjica and Lasva. All the soldiers who were captured that day, I saw them in one classroom. They were all HVO soldiers who were in one classroom in Lasva. Maybe 10 or 15 minutes later, since my wife wanted to see me, I didn't know anything about the civilians, and then they allowed me to come out for about ten minutes to another classroom to see my wife. I saw my wife and my children and my mother, and all the other civilians who were also escorted to the school after us. They were in another classroom in the elementary school in Lasva. Just then, after spending about 15 minutes with my wife, none of the civilians knew anything, so I told my wife about everything that had happened, and I said: You should know, because I didn't know what would happen to me, whether I would survive or not, and I told my wife everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kegelj, do you recall approximately what time it was that you arrived at the Lasva elementary school on the evening of the 26th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: I think it was about 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told the Trial Chamber that you were in a room with other HVO soldiers. Do you recall approximately how many HVO soldiers were in that classroom?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: I think I know exactly. There were 26 of them. Because all HVO soldiers from that classroom were then escorted to the KP Dom in Zenica. I think there was a total of 26 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did the 26 HVO soldiers remain in the Lasva elementary school on that evening?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: I think it was from 10.00 until 1.00 a.m., and I think at about 1.00 a.m., a special police unit from Zenica arrived, as far as I know, some 30 of them, they came to fetch us and one by one, we came out of the classroom. They escorted us. There were about 30 of them. They came with a bus. The bus was at the railway station, and the distance from the school to the railway station is about 700 or 600 metres. And escorted by them, we went to the bus. And along the way, they beat us a lot, in the back, in the stomach, all over, along that route, for some 20 minutes or so. And I know that as we climbed onto the bus one by one, we were ordered to sit down on one side of the bus only, on the left-hand side, whereas the right-hand side was empty. Then they ordered one of the soldiers, Zeljko Cvijanovic, an HVO soldier, to come out. I don't remember what happened. I couldn't see what was going on outside. It was dark. I think they beat him for 10 to 15 minutes. Then they shoved him back in. So he lay on the floor of the bus. He couldn't get up. Then the trip from Lasva to Zenica, it's a distance of some 16 or 17 kilometres, and throughout that journey, this special police, some 30 of them, or 25, we had to bend our heads down, as low as we could, so that we wouldn't see who was beating us. Throughout the trip to Zenica, we were beaten. I received most blows to the back of my head then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kegelj, while you were on the bus, were you informed as to where you were going?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: They told us that they were taking us to Zenica, but all the time they were saying: You are going to the music school. That is what they kept repeating. As far as I can recollect, the driver of the bus was a Croat, and they cursed him, his -- and they ordered him to drive as slowly as possible. They kept saying that they would take us to the music school. They repeated this many times. I don't remember who ordered what, or when, but in any case, we reached the KP Dom by bus. We didn't go to the music school, but to the correctional penitentiary institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your leave, I have about two more questions for the witness and then that would complete the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kegelj, approximately what time did you arrive at the Zenica KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: I think it was after midnight, maybe 2.00 or 2.30 a.m. I didn't have a watch on me, so I can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I take it that would be on the 27th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My final question for you, Mr. Kegelj: You told us that three of the people who were shot outside your garage were Vinko Kegelj, Niko Kegelj, and Stipo Kegelj. Were those three individuals related to you; and if so, how were they related to you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA KEGELJ
utterances.text: Yes. Stipo Kegelj is my uncle. Niko Kegelj is my uncle, and Vinko Kegelj is my uncle. All three are my uncles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kegelj. The Prosecution has no further questions on direct examination, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In view of the time, unfortunately, Witness, you will have to come back tomorrow morning. I know that you have been here for some time, but unless the Defence has no questions -- Has the Defence questions? I assume you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we do have a brief cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So because the Defence has some questions for you, I will ask you to come back tomorrow morning. You will go to your hotel now and you will appear in the morning, which will be at 9.00, when we will see you again, tomorrow morning at 9.00. I will ask Madam Usher to accompany you out of the courtroom now. Before that -- just a moment, please. Sit down. Put your headphones on, please. The Chamber wishes to thank you for the effort that you have made to answer the questions, and we hope you will rest well overnight, so as to be able to answer questions from the Defence tomorrow. So I bid you good night and a pleasant evening. I ask the usher to accompany you outside the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, the time being 5 past after our normal adjournment, I invite the parties to come back tomorrow morning, when we will begin at 9.00 a.m., and we have two witnesses Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.
